Reddit blasts Australia's 'inept' social media ban as court challenge begins

Reddit and a libertarian advocacy group have taken to the High Court to contest the Australian law, which bans large social media platforms from letting under-16s have an account.

CANBERRA: Australia's world-first teen social media ban was "ill thought out" and amounted to a "profound restriction on political debate", a lawyer for messaging platform Reddit told the country's top court in the first legal challenge to the law.  Reddit and a libertarian advocacy group have taken to the High Court to contest the Australian law, which bans large social media platforms from letting under-16s have an account and took effect in late 2025 amid support from parents and opposition from the tech firms. A successful challenge could usher in more opposition from affected companies and slow a global uptake of similar policies as lawmakers from Britain to Malaysia roll out the measures in an effort to protect youth mental and physical health.

Related:

Tiered social media access preferred over outright ban, but is it enough to keep teens safe?

Social media bans for teens: What Talking Point learnt from Australia, Malaysia

The Australian government and its communications minister, a named defendant, have said they will defend the law.

Addressing the court, Perry Herzfeld, for Reddit, said barring under-16s from holding social media accounts stopped them from creating or responding to content on what he called the most important means of communication in the modern world. "That is a very profound restriction on political debate in Australia," Herzfeld said. "There is a very substantial restriction on what young people can now do." Reddit agreed with the Australians' harm-minimisation aim but the law failed to do so, Herzfeld said, terming the legislation "ill thought out" and "inept" since it did not call for any specific measure to keep out minors and failed to restrict other online services where cyberbullying took place, such as gaming websites. While social media content could typically only be created or commented on by logged-in account-holders, vast amounts of material were visible to people with no account, he said. "If the Commonwealth is worried about particular features (of social media), it should regulate the features, which it has not done," he said.

Related:

‘Social media is like fire’: Some wish Indonesia’s planned social media ban for youths can come sooner

‘Be the one in control’: Why are more countries leaning towards banning social media access for kids?

Since the ban went live, multiple studies, including by Australian regulator the eSafety Commissioner, have found that most of the country's teenagers under the cutoff age continue to use social media. The government has since doubled the maximum fine for non-compliance to A$99 million (US$69.5 million), given the eSafety Commissioner greater discovery powers, and said it is preparing an enforcement lawsuit against some of the biggest platforms.

Source: Reuters/ia

HULL: A British adventurer who has been walking around the world for almost three decades is due to finish his trek on Monday (Nov 2), ending a 31,000-mile journey at the house where he grew up. Karl Bushby has hacked through jungles in Central America, crossed the ice between Alaska and Russia and last month swam across the English Channel on the final stretch of a voyage made entirely under his own steam. Hundreds of cheering supporters greeted the 57-year-old in the square of his home city of Hull on Monday morning. "After 28 years, you just couldn't ask for more than this," he told the crowd, before pushing on with his few possessions in a trolley, a spare tyre which will now never be needed slung on top.

"I guess I'll be seeing you around," he added. He then headed for his family home where his mother, his 36-year-old son and a 12-year-old granddaughter were waiting. Bushby served in the British Army's Parachute Regiment in his twenties. After the breakdown of his marriage he drew a line on a world map and set off, inspired by his father who had wondered if it was possible to walk from London to New York. Carrying a tent, a few hundred dollars and a cheap plastic camera, he started in Chile and headed north through the Americas, crossing from Alaska to Russia, Mongolia and China, and back through Europe after swimming the Caspian Sea. "Sometimes the monotony is incredible. You're in deserts and the landscape doesn't change for days to weeks. That can get a little mind-bending. The same with the Arctic," he told Reuters last year.

Explorer Karl Bushby reunites with his mum, Angela, dad, Keith and son, Adam, as they welcome him home after a 28-year walk around the world, in Hull, Britain on Nov 2, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Temilade Adelaja)

He originally expected to spend about 10 years on the road but he hadn't anticipated the obstacles he'd face, amongst them a brief imprisonment in Panama, being held at gunpoint in Mexico and detention by Russian authorities for crossing the border illegally, not to mention delays from the 2008 financial crisis and the COVID pandemic. "This is what an odyssey in the 21st century looks like," he told the Telegraph newspaper. "Half of it is literally dealing with these bureaucratic geopolitical problems, not just the environmental hurdles. There are some times where the solution is just to wait." Bushby told the BBC he has only spent about 15 of the 28 years walking, returning to Mexico periodically to sort out visas, logistics and corporate and media sponsorship deals. A feature-length documentary about his journey is in production, and Bushby is planning to embark on a speaking tour around England in the coming weeks.

Source: Reuters/nh

WASHINGTON: The National Transportation Safety Board said on Monday (Nov 2) that a Learjet 60 that crashed on Sunday in a residential area in Palm Beach County, Florida, killing all nine people on board, may have broken up before hitting the ground at high speed. The private Bombardier-made jet had taken off from Austin, Texas, and was headed to the Bahamas. Heavy rainfall and thunderstorms were occurring in the area where it went down. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, posting on X, highlighted the harrowing experience of those on the aircraft, including the 20-year-old copilot. "She was doing her job, communicating with (air traffic control) right to the end in a terrifying situation," Isaacman wrote. "She likely knew before many of those calls that she was going to die."

A jet can break up in midair at very high rates of descent, subjecting passengers to extreme physical forces.

Videos on social media showed the jet slamming into the ground next to a road and exploding. The pilots reported ice at 10,668m but then reported the plane was descending at a rate of 10,000 feet per minute, which quickly increased to 22,000 feet per minute. "The weather conditions are a major focus of the investigation," NTSB board member Tom Chapman said. Maintenance records indicate a cockpit voice recorder was installed on the jet, but investigators do not know whether it was still on board, he added. The crash left a massive crater by the road near the entrance to a mobile home park, which was partially filled with water because of the severe storms, Chapman said. "We do have some evidence that there was some breakup of the aircraft before impact," he said. "We may find parts of the aircraft some distance away from the actual impact site." TMZ identified the passengers as a Texas tech entrepreneur and his family, a nanny and two close friends, along with two pilots.

Source: Reuters/nh

FAST

SAN FRANCISCO : Apple warned on Monday (Nov 2) that the cost of memory chips would continue to rise, pressuring gross margin for the crucial holiday quarter, but said it had taken steps to lock in supplies. Shares, little changed in after-hours trading after fiscal fourth-quarter results beat expectations, fell 4 per cent during a conference call after executives outlined the weaker outlook, but later pared losses to a 2 per cent decline. Early demand for the iPhone 18 Pro lineup and higher prices boosted the quarter. Apple said it expects gross margin of 45 per cent to 46 per cent in the quarter ending in December, down from 47.9 per cent in the fourth quarter. It forecast services revenue growth of 8 per cent to 9 per cent, below analysts' expectations of 10.7 per cent. The results come as Apple experiments with a string of firsts under new CEO John Ternus, who took over in September. After nearly two decades of launching most new iPhones each autumn, Apple this year is spacing them out, with iPhone Pro and Duo models shipping this year and other models expected next year.

Apple also released a bevy of new non-iPhone products this quarter, including its first touchscreen laptops and first smart-home hub. The steady drumbeat of releases, analysts said, is meant to smooth out Apple's yearly revenue cycle, which for decades showed a huge holiday-quarter boom that petered out by late summer. Apple in recent weeks has grappled with customer reports of cracked screens on the iPhone Duo, its first foldable phone, which sold out within hours online and spurred lines at stores last month. Fiscal fourth-quarter sales were US$114.48 billion, above analyst estimates of US$113.39 billion, according to LSEG data. Profit was US$2.10 per share, above estimates of US$1.99 even when excluding 5 cents from tariff refunds. IPHONE DUO SUPPLY CONSTRAINTS In an interview with Reuters, Ternus said "a very small percentage" of iPhone Duo units had been returned for display issues and that Apple is replacing them. He said the company is overall unable to meet demand, with no timeline for catching up. "Duo is constrained as of today," Ternus said. "The ramp is going well ... but at this point, we're not able to predict when supply and demand will be in balance." Fourth-quarter iPhone sales, which included iPhone 18 Pro models but not Duo, were US$57.58 billion, above estimates of US$56.54 billion, according to LSEG data. The staggered launch strategy comes as Apple faces headwinds from an AI-driven memory-chip price spike that could dampen the margin boost Apple derives from storage upgrades. "The big question for Apple moving forward will be how well they can weather the significant component price increases that have slowed their PC and smartphone competitors," said Bob O'Donnell, chief analyst at TECHnalysis Research.  "The new iPhone Duo looks to be a big hit, but the company has to solve the screen glitches and ramp up its manufacturing output." PRICE RISES OFFSET CHIP COSTS As it launched the iPhone 18 Pro, Apple also raised iPhone 17 prices by US$100 and increased some MacBook prices, softening the blow of rising memory costs. "We did see higher memory costs as compared to the June quarter, which was partially offset by the benefit of carrying inventory and lower costs on certain non-memory components," Ternus said. "These price increases provided some offset." Fourth-quarter gross margins were 47.9 per cent, above estimates of 47.5 per cent, according to LSEG data. On the investor call, Chief Financial Officer Kevan Parekh said Apple expects memory costs to keep rising into next year. Asked whether Apple had signed a long-term supply agreement, Chief Operating Officer Sabih Khan did not directly confirm a deal but said Apple is working closely with memory suppliers and that its purchasing commitments increased by US$33 billion during the quarter. Shares of memory-chip maker Micron rose more than 1 per cent in after-hours trading on Monday, and shares of chip-manufacturing equipment makers KLA and Applied Materials also rose. Apple also pointed to Siri AI, which runs partially in Google's cloud, as a factor impacting margins. The company plans to charge more for iCloud+ subscriptions to offset AI costs, though it has not rolled out specific pricing. "There are going to be some usage limits on features that rely on server-side models, which include Siri AI and intelligent photo editing," Ternus said during the call. Mac sales were $10.79 billion, above estimates of US$9.61 billion. Services revenue was US$31.57 billion, in line with estimates of US$31.58 billion. iPad and wearables sales were US$6.23 billion and US$8.30 billion, both below estimates. Chinese sales were US$17.54 billion, below the US$18.58 billion analysts estimated, according to Visible Alpha data.

Source: Reuters/nh

ROME: Italians on Monday (Nov 2) celebrated the success of Kimi Antonelli, who became Formula 1's youngest world champion at the age of 20 when he clinched the title in Mexico City. Antonelli, who is from the northern city of Bologna, is also the first Italian champion since 1953. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni took to social media to praise what she called an "extraordinary achievement". "A success that puts an Italian driver back on top of the world, rewarding talent, commitment, determination and dedication," Meloni said.

"It's a source of great pride for our country," she wrote on X, alongside a picture of Antonelli holding the Italian flag. La Gazzetta dello Sport newspaper ran the headline "Kimitico", a play on words meaning "Legendary Kimi". La Stampa newspaper struck a similar tone, with its headline "Kimi nella leggenda" ("Kimi makes history.")  In Rome, locals took delight in an Italian sporting success, with one comparing Antonelli to tennis champion Jannik Sinner. "They're two shining stars of Italian sport," said Daniela Bulgarini. "He seems like a good kid, very talented. Talent and hard work always pay off."

Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli celebrates with an Italian flag on the podium after finishing third in the Mexico City Grand Prix and clinching the 2026 Formula 1 World Championship. (Photo: Reuters/Eloisa Sanchez)

DESTINED FOR THE TOP Antonelli, who drives for Mercedes, is the son of a sports car racing father who took him to the track as a young boy. He was taken on by Mercedes as an 11-year-old karter when his potential as a Formula 1 driver was apparent. "After such a long time without an Italian winning, whether with Ferrari or with other teams, other constructors, it's certainly a great thing," said Giovanni, a worker in Rome. Several hundred fans watched a screening of the grand prix late on Sunday at the Checco Costa Museum at the Imola F1 race track. Although Imola is the home track of the Ferrari team, fans put that allegiance to one side to cheer for Antonelli whose third-place finish in Mexico was enough to seal the title. Another watch-party was held in a cinema in Bologna. The local Serie A soccer club joined in the celebrations, with a post on X reading "The whole of Bologna is proud of you".
